description: Machine learning as the substrate understands it — not to do, but to know why. The substrate's existing neural_networks + gadgets Mts let it AUTHOR networks from declarative specification (Tracr-with-the-human-removed); training is a different paradigm. This Mt covers: what training IS (backprop, SGD, optimizers, loss landscape, regularization), what modern ML architectures are (CNN, RNN, Transformer, attention, embeddings), the training pipeline (data loaders, batching, hyperparameter search), transfer learning + fine-tuning + RLHF, inference optimisation, and the failure modes (hallucination, distribution shift, adversarial). Plus the substrate's grounded critique of the paradigm: training is brute-force search through weight space, statistical fit isn't symbolic understanding, opacity is a feature of the approach. The substrate knows ML; the substrate is not ML.
category_inheritance: genlMt → compiler_theory + neural_networks + gadgets. The cost-equivalence vocabulary applies to compute requirements; denotational equivalence captures the gap between what training optimises for (loss) vs what's intended (capability). The substrate's authored-network Mt (gadgets) provides the alternative paradigm reference.

concepts.name: supervised_learning
concepts.definition: Train a model on (input, output) pairs. Loss measures distance between model output + ground truth; gradient descent minimises loss.
concepts.why: Dominant ML paradigm. Works when labelled data is plentiful. Cost: labelled data is expensive; model fits the distribution of training data (not the underlying truth). Statistical correlation, not understanding.

concepts.name: unsupervised_learning
concepts.definition: Train on unlabelled data. Loss measures internal structure: reconstruction (autoencoders), clustering, contrastive (similar examples close).
concepts.why: Data without labels is abundant. Learns representations that may be useful for downstream tasks. No truth signal; learns whatever structure the data has. The 'understanding' is whatever the loss happens to reward.

concepts.name: self_supervised_learning
concepts.definition: Mask part of the input; train model to predict the missing part. BERT (masked language modeling), GPT (next-token prediction), MAE (masked autoencoder).
concepts.why: Foundation of LLM pretraining. Generates infinite supervised tasks from unlabelled data. The model learns to fill in blanks — useful proxy for general capability, but not the same as it.

concepts.name: reinforcement_learning
concepts.definition: Agent acts in environment, receives reward. Goal: maximise cumulative reward. Q-learning, policy gradients, actor-critic.
concepts.why: Sequential decision-making. Sparse reward + exploration are hard problems. AlphaGo, robotics, RLHF for LLMs. Reward shaping is its own field — wrong reward = wrong agent.

concepts.name: loss_function
concepts.definition: Function measuring how wrong the model is. Output: scalar to minimise. Examples: MSE, cross-entropy, contrastive, KL divergence.
concepts.why: The training target. Whatever the loss measures becomes what the model optimises for — including the gap between that and what humans wanted. 'Reward hacking' = optimising the loss in ways that don't match intent.

concepts.name: mean_squared_error
concepts.definition: MSE: average of (prediction - target)². Standard for regression.
concepts.why: Differentiable everywhere; gradient is clean. Penalises large errors quadratically. Sensitive to outliers. Default regression loss; alternatives (Huber, MAE) handle outliers better.

concepts.name: cross_entropy_loss
concepts.definition: For classification: -log(probability assigned to correct class). Equivalent to maximum likelihood.
concepts.why: Standard classification loss. Combines softmax + log naturally (numerically stable LogSoftmax). Penalises confident wrong predictions heavily.

concepts.name: kl_divergence
concepts.definition: KL(P||Q): how much information lost when approximating P with Q. Asymmetric.
concepts.why: Used in variational inference (ELBO loss), distillation (student matches teacher), GAN training. Information-theoretic distance between distributions.

concepts.name: contrastive_loss
concepts.definition: Pull similar pairs (same class) closer; push dissimilar pairs apart in embedding space. InfoNCE, triplet loss.
concepts.why: Self-supervised learning core. SimCLR, MoCo, CLIP. Learns useful representations from labels-free data via similarity structure.

concepts.name: gradient_descent
concepts.definition: Move weights in direction opposite to gradient of loss. New weight = old weight - learning_rate × gradient.
concepts.why: Local search through weight space. Provably converges to local minimum under convex loss; ML losses are non-convex. Works empirically; theory doesn't fully explain why deep networks reach good minima.

concepts.name: stochastic_gradient_descent
concepts.definition: SGD: gradient computed on mini-batch, not full dataset. Noisy gradient but cheap per step.
concepts.why: Practical: full-batch gradient on millions of examples is too expensive. Noise also helps escape sharp minima (which generalise poorly). Modern default; momentum + Adam refinements built on SGD.

concepts.name: momentum
concepts.definition: Exponential moving average of past gradients. Update uses (1-β)·new_grad + β·old_velocity.
concepts.why: Smooths gradient noise. Accelerates in consistent directions; damps oscillations. β ≈ 0.9 standard.

concepts.name: Adam_optimizer
concepts.definition: Adaptive Moment Estimation: per-parameter learning rate from running mean + variance of gradients. Default LR 1e-3.
concepts.why: Works out-of-box on many problems. Most popular optimiser. Cost: 2 extra state tensors per param. Sometimes worse generalisation than SGD with momentum.

concepts.name: AdamW
concepts.definition: Adam + decoupled weight decay. Weight decay subtracted from weights directly, not added to gradient.
concepts.why: Standard for modern training. Adam's L2 regularisation was effectively absorbed by adaptive LR; AdamW separates concerns. Used in nearly all LLM pretraining.

concepts.name: learning_rate
concepts.definition: Scaling factor for gradient step. Too high: oscillation, divergence. Too low: slow convergence.
concepts.why: Most-tuned hyperparameter. Modern training uses warmup + decay schedules. Mismatched LR = wasted training run.

concepts.name: learning_rate_schedule
concepts.definition: How LR changes over training. Linear warmup, cosine decay, step decay, constant.
concepts.why: Warmup avoids early instability; decay refines convergence. Modern LLMs: linear warmup (1-5%) + cosine decay to ~10% of peak. The schedule matters as much as the peak LR.

concepts.name: backpropagation
concepts.definition: Algorithm: chain rule applied through computational graph. Computes gradient of loss w.r.t. every parameter.
concepts.why: Foundation of training. Forward pass computes loss; backward pass computes gradients. O(n) cost in network size — what makes training tractable.

concepts.name: automatic_differentiation
concepts.definition: Compute derivatives from program structure, not numerical approximation. Forward + reverse modes; reverse = backprop.
concepts.why: PyTorch + TensorFlow + JAX all do reverse-mode autodiff. Trace operations; replay backwards with chain rule. Lets researchers write models in regular code; framework handles gradients.

concepts.name: regularization
concepts.definition: Add term to loss penalising complexity. L2 (weight decay) is most common.
concepts.why: Reduces overfitting. Hyperparameter trades training fit against generalisation. Modern: weight decay + dropout + data augmentation often together.

concepts.name: dropout
concepts.definition: At training time: randomly zero a fraction of activations. At test time: use all, scale down.
concepts.why: Prevents co-adaptation. Acts as ensemble over many sub-networks. Reduces overfitting. Cost: noisier training. Less used in modern LLMs (Transformer + heavy data work without).

concepts.name: batch_normalization
concepts.definition: Normalise activations within mini-batch: subtract mean, divide by std, learnable scale + shift.
concepts.why: Stabilises training; enables higher LR. Standard in CNNs. Issues: batch-size dependent (small batch = noisy stats); replaced by LayerNorm in Transformers.

concepts.name: layer_normalization
concepts.definition: Normalise activations across feature dimension, per sample. Independent of batch.
concepts.why: Standard in Transformers. Batch-independent: works for RL, online learning, batch size 1. LayerNorm + residual is the backbone of modern architectures.

concepts.name: weight_decay
concepts.definition: Add λ·||W||² to loss; equivalently, subtract λ·W from each gradient step.
concepts.why: Encourages smaller weights → simpler functions. Standard regularizer. Modern: AdamW separates from gradient.

concepts.name: early_stopping
concepts.definition: Stop training when validation loss stops improving. Save best checkpoint.
concepts.why: Cheap regularisation. Acts like implicit constraint on training compute. Many production runs use; LLM pretraining uses fixed schedules instead.

concepts.name: data_augmentation
concepts.definition: Synthetic variants of training data: crop, rotate, flip (images); paraphrase, masking (text).
concepts.why: Increases effective training set; reduces overfitting; bakes in invariances. Critical for limited data. ImageNet's flip/crop augmentation single largest improvement of an era.

concepts.name: multilayer_perceptron
concepts.definition: MLP: stack of fully-connected layers with non-linearities. The original 'neural network'.
concepts.why: Universal approximator. Foundation. Most modern architectures still contain MLP blocks. Limited inductive bias — needs many parameters to handle structured data.

concepts.name: convolutional_neural_network
concepts.definition: CNN: stack of convolutional layers exploiting translation invariance. Pooling reduces spatial resolution.
concepts.why: Dominant for vision 2012-2020. Strong inductive bias: nearby pixels related. AlexNet, VGG, ResNet, EfficientNet. Largely replaced by Vision Transformers but still used in efficient deployment.

concepts.name: recurrent_neural_network
concepts.definition: RNN: hidden state updated each step from previous state + current input. Processes sequences.
concepts.why: Pre-Transformer sequence modelling standard. Vanilla RNN trains poorly (vanishing gradients). LSTM/GRU fix this. Largely replaced by Transformer for NLP; survives in some streaming/online contexts.

concepts.name: LSTM
concepts.definition: Long Short-Term Memory. Gated RNN with forget/input/output gates + cell state. Hochreiter+Schmidhuber 1997.
concepts.why: Tractable training for long sequences. Standard for sequence modelling before Transformer. Still used in some applications (small/mobile).

concepts.name: Transformer_architecture
concepts.definition: Vaswani 2017 'Attention is All You Need'. Stack of self-attention + MLP blocks. Encoder-decoder or decoder-only.
concepts.why: Foundation of modern LLMs. Parallel processing of sequences (unlike RNN). Scales massively. GPT, BERT, T5, LLaMA all variants. The architecture of the 2020s.

concepts.name: self_attention
concepts.definition: Each position attends to all positions. Query, key, value linear projections; attention = softmax(QK^T / √d) V.
concepts.why: Captures any-distance dependencies. The Transformer's core. Quadratic in sequence length — bottleneck for long contexts. Modern: efficient attention variants (Flash, sparse, linear).

concepts.name: multi_head_attention
concepts.definition: Split Q/K/V into multiple heads; each head attends independently. Concatenate outputs.
concepts.why: Different heads attend to different relationships (syntactic, semantic, positional). More expressive than single attention. Standard ~8-32 heads.

concepts.name: positional_encoding
concepts.definition: Add position information to embeddings. Sinusoidal (Vaswani), learned, or rotary (RoPE).
concepts.why: Attention is order-agnostic; positional encoding restores sequence order. RoPE (rotary position embedding) standard in modern LLMs — supports extrapolation beyond training length.

concepts.name: token_embedding
concepts.definition: Map discrete tokens to dense vectors. Learnable matrix of vocab_size × embed_dim.
concepts.why: Bridges discrete (token id) to continuous (vector). Carries semantic similarity. Embeddings often shared between input + output (tied embeddings) for efficiency.

concepts.name: feed_forward_network_transformer
concepts.definition: Per-position MLP within transformer block. Typically: Linear(d → 4d), GeLU, Linear(4d → d).
concepts.why: Where most parameters live. Per-token nonlinear transformation. GeLU more stable than ReLU for deep transformers.

concepts.name: residual_connection
concepts.definition: Output = layer(input) + input. Identity shortcut alongside transformation.
concepts.why: Enables training very deep networks. Gradient flows directly through skip path. ResNet's central innovation; standard in Transformers.

concepts.name: tokenization
concepts.definition: Convert text to sequence of tokens (subword units). BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece.
concepts.why: Foundation of text-based LLM. Tokens are not words; they're statistical units. Different tokenizers → different model behaviour. Number-handling, code, multilingual all sensitive.

concepts.name: byte_pair_encoding
concepts.definition: BPE: iteratively merge most-frequent character pair. Tokens are merge sequences.
concepts.why: Standard tokenizer for GPT family. Handles rare words via sub-tokens. ~50K typical vocab. The 'GPT-2 tokenizer' specifically.

concepts.name: dataset_split
concepts.definition: Train (~80%) / validation (~10%) / test (~10%). Train: model fits. Validation: hyperparameter tuning. Test: final eval.
concepts.why: Hold out data unseen during training. Validation drives decisions; test honestly measures final performance. Mixing them = test set contamination.

concepts.name: mini_batch_training
concepts.definition: Process N examples in parallel; average gradient; update weights. N is batch size.
concepts.why: GPU efficiency: parallel matrix ops. Larger batch = less noise + more parallelism + harder generalisation. Modern LLMs use ~1M-token batches.

concepts.name: gradient_accumulation
concepts.definition: Compute gradients on micro-batches; accumulate before weight update. Effective batch = micro_batch × accumulation_steps.
concepts.why: Train with larger effective batch than fits in memory. Common for LLMs where 1M-token batches don't fit on one GPU.

concepts.name: distributed_training
concepts.definition: Train across multiple GPUs/nodes. Data parallel (each GPU sees subset), model parallel (each GPU holds subset of weights).
concepts.why: Scale beyond single device. Modern LLMs need both. NCCL for GPU comms; Horovod, PyTorch DDP, FSDP. Communication often the bottleneck.

concepts.name: checkpoint
concepts.definition: Saved model + optimiser state. Allows resuming training, deployment, distillation.
concepts.why: Long training runs need restart capability (failures, preemption). Optimiser state (Adam moments) crucial for continuing — small fraction of model size but essential.

concepts.name: hyperparameter_search
concepts.definition: Grid search, random search, Bayesian optimisation, evolutionary. Find best (LR, batch, dropout, etc.).
concepts.why: Optimiser is fixed; hyperparameters tune the loss landscape's trajectory. Expensive: each trial = full training run. Modern: scaling laws + transfer reduce blind search.

concepts.name: pretraining
concepts.definition: Train base model on broad unsupervised data. LLMs: predict next token over web-scale text.
concepts.why: Compute-heavy upstream step. Yields general-capability base model. Cost: 1M+ GPU-hours for frontier models. Pretrained weights distribute (HuggingFace) for downstream use.

concepts.name: fine_tuning
concepts.definition: Continue training pretrained model on task-specific data. Updates all (or selected) weights.
concepts.why: Adapts general model to specific task. Cheap compared to pretraining. Risk: catastrophic forgetting of pretraining knowledge. Standard transfer learning approach.

concepts.name: LoRA
concepts.definition: Low-Rank Adaptation. Freeze base weights; train low-rank decomposition added to each weight matrix.
concepts.why: Memory-efficient fine-tuning: <1% extra parameters. Multiple task-specific adapters can swap on same base. Standard in LLM fine-tuning, image diffusion.

concepts.name: instruction_tuning
concepts.definition: Fine-tune base LLM on (instruction, response) pairs. Teaches model to follow instructions.
concepts.why: Bridges raw-text pretraining (predict next token) to user-facing (respond to instructions). Standard step before deployment.

concepts.name: RLHF
concepts.definition: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. Train reward model on human preferences; use PPO to optimise LLM against reward model.
concepts.why: Aligns model to human preferences beyond what's expressible as labels. ChatGPT's secret sauce. Cost: human labellers + multi-stage training. Reward hacking + sycophancy emerge.

concepts.name: PPO
concepts.definition: Proximal Policy Optimization. Schulman 2017. Policy gradient with clipped objective preventing too-large updates.
concepts.why: Stable RL training. Standard for RLHF. Clipping prevents destructive updates; trust region without expensive Hessian.

concepts.name: DPO
concepts.definition: Direct Preference Optimization. Trains LLM directly on preference data without reward model.
concepts.why: Simpler than PPO+reward model. Comparable results. Used heavily for open-source LLM tuning (LLaMA derivatives).

concepts.name: constitutional_AI
concepts.definition: Anthropic's approach: model critiques + revises own outputs against constitution. RLAIF (RL from AI Feedback) instead of human.
concepts.why: Scale: humans can't label every example. AI feedback bootstrapped from initial human-labelled examples. Used in Claude training.

concepts.name: quantization_ML
concepts.definition: Reduce weight precision: float32 → int8 (4x), int4 (8x). Inference-only or quantization-aware training.
concepts.why: Inference cost dominates production. 4x smaller models, 2-4x faster inference. Quality loss: ~1-2% on int8, more on int4. Critical for edge deployment.

concepts.name: knowledge_distillation
concepts.definition: Train small student model to match large teacher's outputs (or intermediate features).
concepts.why: Compresses big model into small one. Student gets soft probabilities (more info than hard labels). Standard for shipping models at scale.

concepts.name: KV_cache
concepts.definition: For autoregressive generation: cache key + value tensors from previous tokens. Avoids recomputing.
concepts.why: Inference cost drops from O(N²) to O(N) per new token. Memory cost: ~2 × layers × heads × head_dim × seq_len. Dominates LLM serving memory.

concepts.name: flash_attention
concepts.definition: Tri Dao 2022. Tiled, online softmax attention computation. Same math, 2-3x faster + lower memory.
concepts.why: Hot-loop optimisation for attention. Standard in modern training + inference. FlashAttention-2 + 3 further improvements. Game-changer for long context.

concepts.name: batched_inference
concepts.definition: Process multiple requests in one forward pass. Continuous batching dynamically adds/removes sequences.
concepts.why: GPU underutilised serving one request. Batching → throughput. vLLM's PagedAttention + continuous batching standardised modern serving.

concepts.name: speculative_decoding
concepts.definition: Use small fast draft model to propose multiple tokens; large target model verifies in parallel.
concepts.why: 2-3x decoding speedup when draft is accurate. Works because target verifies cheaply (one forward pass for multiple tokens). Standard in modern serving.

concepts.name: scaling_laws
concepts.definition: Kaplan + Chinchilla: loss is a power law of compute / parameters / data. Optimal scaling has all three growing together.
concepts.why: Predicts training curves. Justifies massive scale. Caveats: extrapolation beyond data range is suspect; 'scaling' specific to current architecture + dataset.

concepts.name: emergent_capabilities
concepts.definition: Capabilities that appear suddenly at certain scale. Reasoning, in-context learning, chain-of-thought.
concepts.why: Discussed as breakthrough phenomena. Schaeffer 2023: emergence often artifact of nonlinear metrics + sparse evaluation. Real curves usually smooth. The 'emergence' narrative oversells.

concepts.name: in_context_learning
concepts.definition: LLM learns from examples in prompt without weight updates. 'Few-shot' or 'zero-shot'.
concepts.why: Surprising capability of scaled transformers. Not understood mechanically. Likely combination of statistical pattern matching + meta-learning during pretraining.

concepts.name: chain_of_thought_prompting
concepts.definition: Prompt model to 'think step by step'. Often improves reasoning on complex tasks.
concepts.why: Trick that works empirically. Allows model to use intermediate computation; doesn't imply understanding. Brittle: rephrasing changes answer.

concepts.name: hallucination_LLM
concepts.definition: Model generates confident but false information. Fabricated citations, wrong facts, made-up names.
concepts.why: Failure mode: model is trained to predict plausible tokens, not factual ones. No grounding in truth. Mitigation: retrieval augmentation, alignment training — but the underlying issue persists.

concepts.name: adversarial_examples
concepts.definition: Inputs crafted to fool model: imperceptible perturbations cause misclassification (vision); jailbreaks for LLMs.
concepts.why: Reveals: model has learned a different function than the human concept. Decision boundaries don't align with semantics. Universal across architectures.

concepts.name: catastrophic_forgetting
concepts.definition: Network trained on task A then task B loses ability on A. Weights rewritten.
concepts.why: Major problem for sequential/continual learning. Mitigations: EWC, replay buffers, mixture of experts. Fundamental to gradient-based training: weights are shared.

concepts.name: distribution_shift
concepts.definition: Inference data distribution differs from training. Performance degrades; calibration breaks.
concepts.why: Test-set performance doesn't transfer to deployment. Common cause of production model failures. ML systems brittle to OOD inputs.

concepts.name: overfitting
concepts.definition: Model memorises training data; performs worse on unseen. Train loss low; validation loss high.
concepts.why: Symptom of capacity > data complexity. Mitigated by regularisation + more data. Modern LLMs interpolate at scale; classical overfitting picture incomplete.

concepts.name: underfitting
concepts.definition: Model too simple to capture data structure. Both train + validation loss high.
concepts.why: Solution: more capacity, better architecture, longer training. Less common in modern over-parameterised regimes.

concepts.name: double_descent
concepts.definition: Generalisation error decreases, increases (classical regime), then decreases again as model size grows past interpolation threshold.
concepts.why: Contradicts classical bias-variance picture. Modern LLMs are in the over-parameterised regime. Mechanism not fully understood.

concepts.name: lottery_ticket_hypothesis
concepts.definition: Frankle 2018: dense networks contain sparse 'winning ticket' subnetworks that train to comparable accuracy.
concepts.why: Implies most weights at training end are redundant. Sparse-from-init networks could in principle match dense. The mechanism behind: gradient descent finds + exploits these.

concepts.name: GPU_training_compute
concepts.definition: Training a frontier LLM: ~10^25 FLOPs, ~$100M cost, months of wall time, MW of power.
concepts.why: Compute scale is the binding constraint. Few labs can pretrain frontier models. Open-source uses smaller (10-100x less) compute. Inference is also expensive (KV cache + matmul).

concepts.name: weight_space_is_opaque
concepts.definition: Trained weights are dense matrices of seemingly-random numbers. What computation they implement is not directly readable.
concepts.why: Interpretability is a research area, not standard practice. Compare to authored networks (Tracr-style) where the algorithm IS the structure. The substrate's gadgets Mt provides networks whose computation is exact + queryable.

concepts.name: statistical_fit_is_not_understanding
concepts.definition: Trained model approximates the function implied by training data. Whether that function is 'understanding' is a category question.
concepts.why: LLM passing exams ≠ LLM understanding the subject. Tests prove statistical similarity to humans-who-pass. Substrate's stance: symbolic structure + provable correctness ≠ statistical fit.

concepts.name: loss_minimisation_isnt_capability_optimisation
concepts.definition: Model optimises whatever the loss measures. If loss measures next-token-prediction, model gets good at next-token-prediction — not at 'being helpful'.
concepts.why: Goodhart's law for ML. Reward hacking, gaming benchmarks, etc. are not bugs — they're loss being optimised correctly. The gap between loss + capability is the entire alignment problem.

concepts.name: training_is_local_search
concepts.definition: SGD performs local search through high-dimensional loss landscape. Finds local minimum.
concepts.why: No guarantee of optimum. Different random seeds → different solutions. Performance is whatever search happens to find, not what's possible. The substrate's authored networks are exact; training's are stochastic.

concepts.name: training_paradigm_brute_force
concepts.definition: Training searches a 10^11-parameter space with no prior structure. Effective only because compute is abundant + data is plentiful.
concepts.why: The 'bitter lesson' (Sutton): compute beats clever algorithms. The substrate disagrees: declarative authoring + symbolic structure with provable properties is a different paradigm. Both work; for different reasons.

concepts.name: Tracr_alternative_authored_nets
concepts.definition: Lindner 2023: compile RASP program to exact transformer weights. Networks designed via specification, not trained.
concepts.why: Substrate's own gadgets Mt instantiates this. Network's behaviour is provably exact (compiled from spec). Polar opposite of training: structure first, weights derived. The substrate's preferred paradigm.

concepts.name: neurosymbolic_AI
concepts.definition: Combine neural networks (statistical pattern recognition) with symbolic reasoning (logic, knowledge graphs).
concepts.why: Acknowledges both approaches have strengths. Used in: AlphaGeometry, theorem proving, knowledge-grounded systems. Substrate's stance: symbolic structure with neural learning where useful.

concepts.name: knowledge_representation
concepts.definition: Symbolic encoding of facts + relationships. Ontologies, semantic networks, frames, microtheories.
concepts.why: Pre-LLM AI's foundation (CYC, RDF, SemWeb). Provides explicit + queryable + provable knowledge. The substrate IS this — microtheories, concepts, rules. Different paradigm; can coexist with ML.

concepts.name: compiled_networks
concepts.definition: Networks generated from declarative specification (Tracr) or symbolic algorithm. Behaviour is provably correct by construction.
concepts.why: Authored, not trained. The substrate's gadgets Mt produces these. No SGD; no random init; no loss function. Direct from understanding to weights.

concepts.name: linear_discriminant_analysis
concepts.definition: Find directions that separate classes by maximising the ratio of BETWEEN-CLASS scatter to WITHIN-CLASS scatter (the Fisher criterion). Project the data onto the discriminant directions; equivalently WHITEN by the within-class covariance so the structured nuisance variation that spreads each class along its own within-class directions is suppressed while the between-class directions are kept.
concepts.why: Removes a structured nuisance SUBSPACE rather than a scalar: a within-class scatter DIRECTION along which a class co-varies (e.g. speaker / channel variation within a word) is cancelled by PROJECTING onto the COMPLEMENT of the within-class scatter — whitening by the within-class covariance (WCCN). Standard for speaker/channel-robust recognition (i-vector LDA/WCCN).

concepts.name: cholesky_whitening
concepts.definition: Whiten a vector by a symmetric positive-definite matrix W: factor W = L Lᵀ (Cholesky decomposition) and forward-solve L y = x, giving y = L⁻¹x whose squared norm ‖y‖² = xᵀ W⁻¹ x is the Mahalanobis distance under W. Equivalent to multiplying by W^(-1/2) for nearest-neighbour purposes.
concepts.why: The matrix FACTORISATION (Cholesky / eigendecomposition) and the triangular SOLVE are primitive linear-algebra operations the DSL lacks (it has Dot/VecAdd/VecSub but no matrix factorisation or inverse). They are what makes within-class WHITENING (the derived cross-speaker fix) computable: suppress the within-class scatter directions by applying L⁻¹.

concepts.name: within_class_scatter
concepts.definition: The within-class scatter (pooled within-class covariance): group the tokens by class, subtract each class mean, and average the outer products (x-μ_c)(x-μ_c)ᵀ over all tokens. A regularized (shrinkage) estimate adds a diagonal load W ← (1-s)W + s·(tr W/d)·I so the d×d matrix is well-conditioned for inversion when tokens are few relative to dimension.
concepts.why: This is the matrix the derived cross-speaker fix WHITENS by — it captures the directions a class spreads along (across speakers). Computing it needs grouped mean-subtraction and an OUTER-PRODUCT accumulation into a d×d matrix, which the DSL lacks (it has Dot/VecAdd/VecSub but no outer product or matrix accumulation). Pairs with cholesky_whitening: scatter then whiten.

concepts.name: covariate_conditioning
concepts.definition: Covariate adjustment / confound regression / batch-effect removal (ComBat): when an OBSERVED attribute (a covariate / confound / batch / site / speaker) explains structured variation that is NOT the target, remove the variation attributable to that KNOWN attribute by building the transform from the OBSERVED attribute grouping — compute the BETWEEN-GROUP scatter across the observed attribute values and project it out (or whiten by it), or regress each feature on the observed attribute and keep the residual.
concepts.why: It needs ONLY the observed attribute labels, NOT the target labels — so it removes a nuisance even when the target is unlabelled (the case within-class whitening cannot handle). The known confound supplies the grouping the discriminant whitening otherwise lacks: between-observed-group removal conditions OUT the nuisance and leaves the target structure as the residual.

concepts.name: between_class_scatter
concepts.definition: The between-class scatter: the scatter of the class MEANS about the global mean, weighted by class size — Sb = (1/N) Σ_c n_c (μ_c - μ)(μ_c - μ)ᵀ. It captures the variation that lies BETWEEN groups (as opposed to within them); with the within-class scatter Sw it decomposes the total scatter St = Sw + Sb.
concepts.why: It is the matrix the nuisance-conditioned fix whitens by when the OBSERVED attribute is the grouping (between-speaker scatter = the variation the speaker explains). Computing it needs per-group means, mean-difference OUTER PRODUCTS weighted by group size, accumulated into a d×d matrix — which the DSL lacks. Pairs with WithinScatter (St = Sw + Sb) and Whiten.

concepts.name: subword_tokenization
concepts.definition: Spell ANY word, including ones never seen as a whole, as a SEQUENCE of a FINITE set of recurring SUB-WORD UNITS (byte-pair / wordpiece pieces). A finite system of parts plus sequencing composes an OPEN-ENDED set of words.
concepts.why: Makes the vocabulary OPEN: a word never encountered as a unit is still producible as a sequence of its parts, instead of an all-or-nothing whole the model either stored or cannot say. The compositional generativity that covers out-of-vocabulary words.

concepts.name: statistical_language_model
concepts.definition: A model of which WORDS tend to FOLLOW which — the probability of the next word given the preceding context (n-gram / sequence model). Predicts the most likely continuation of a word sequence.
concepts.why: Lets a DOUBTFUL or missing word be RECOVERED from its surrounding words: the context predicts/restores the uncertain item, so recognition uses which words follow which rather than each word in isolation.

rules.name: loss_function_defines_capability
if: a model is trained to minimise loss L
then: it becomes good at whatever L measures, not what was intended
rules.why: Goodhart's law. If L = next-token prediction on internet text, model becomes a next-token predictor — useful for some tasks, deceptively similar to many capabilities, not actually any of them. The choice of L IS the choice of capability.

rules.name: gradient_descent_local_search
if: weights are updated by SGD
then: the trained network is a local minimum of the loss landscape
rules.why: No guarantee of optimality. Different initialisations → different solutions. Performance is whatever search happens to find. The substrate's authored networks (gadgets Mt) are exact — no stochastic search.

rules.name: compute_data_parameters_scale_together
if: one of compute / data / params is scaled without others
then: loss reduction is suboptimal (Chinchilla)
rules.why: Hoffmann 2022. For fixed compute budget, optimal allocation has params and data growing proportionally. GPT-3 over-parameterised vs Chinchilla; LLaMA family followed Chinchilla scaling.

rules.name: regularisation_required_for_generalisation
if: model has more parameters than training examples
then: some form of regularisation is required to avoid overfitting
rules.why: Without regularisation: memorise training, fail on test. Weight decay + dropout + data augmentation + early stopping + (implicit) SGD noise all regularise. Modern LLMs interpolate but still need regularisation.

rules.name: Adam_works_out_of_box_SGD_better_at_optimum
if: model is being tuned with default hyperparameters
then: Adam is the practical choice
rules.why: Adam's adaptive LR handles most loss landscapes without tuning. SGD + momentum sometimes generalises better with careful LR schedule. Standard: Adam for exploration, SGD for production polish on vision; Adam everywhere for NLP.

rules.name: transformer_O_n2_in_sequence_length
if: self-attention is applied to sequence of length N
then: compute + memory are O(N²)
rules.why: Each token attends to every other. Quadratic in N. Long context (100K+) requires efficient attention (Flash, sparse, linear). The fundamental scaling bottleneck.

rules.name: LoRA_low_rank_captures_task_adaptation
if: fine-tuning task is similar to pretraining
then: low-rank update captures most of the adaptation
rules.why: Empirical: task-specific changes are low-dimensional. Rank-4 to rank-16 LoRA matches full fine-tuning on many tasks. <1% extra params. Standard for LLM fine-tuning.

rules.name: RLHF_aligns_to_preferences_not_truth
if: model is trained via RLHF
then: it learns to produce outputs the reward model rates highly
rules.why: Reward model is a learned approximation of human preferences. Model optimises that approximation. Sycophancy + reward hacking emerge. The gap between 'good reward' and 'good behaviour' is the alignment problem.

rules.name: quantization_trades_precision_for_efficiency
if: weights are quantised to 8 or 4 bit
then: model is 2-8x smaller + faster at <2% quality loss
rules.why: Most weights don't need float32 precision. Outliers (a few large values) cause most quantization error; mixed precision (FP32 outliers + INT8 rest) recovers quality. Critical for deployment.

rules.name: KV_cache_makes_autoregressive_decoding_tractable
if: autoregressive generation caches K + V tensors
then: per-token cost is O(N) instead of O(N²)
rules.why: Without cache: recompute attention over full prefix every token. With cache: only new token's attention. The reason long-context generation is tractable. Memory cost is the new bottleneck.

rules.name: hallucination_inherent_to_unsupervised_generation
if: model is trained to generate plausible tokens
then: it produces confident-sounding falsehoods
rules.why: Training signal is 'predict next token in this corpus'. Plausibility ≈ training distribution similarity. No truth signal. RAG + retrieval mitigates; doesn't eliminate. The substrate's symbolic knowledge provides an alternative: graph-resident facts are verifiable.

rules.name: adversarial_examples_reveal_model_function_gap
if: small perturbation causes large output change
then: model's learned function differs from the human concept
rules.why: Image recognition: pixels we'd ignore can flip classification. LLM jailbreaks: prompts that bypass safety training. The decision boundary doesn't align with semantic boundary. Universal across architectures.

rules.name: distribution_shift_breaks_deployed_models
if: test distribution differs from training distribution
then: accuracy + calibration degrade
rules.why: Models interpolate training data. Out-of-distribution is extrapolation. Production data drifts; models trained yesterday fail today. Continual training + monitoring + retraining is the ML ops loop.

rules.name: scaling_laws_predict_but_dont_explain
if: compute / data / params are scaled together
then: loss follows a power law decline
rules.why: Empirical fit. Useful for budgeting + planning. Doesn't explain mechanism. Extrapolation beyond data is risky. Doesn't predict capability emergence (Schaeffer 2023 suggests emergence is partly metric artifact).

rules.name: trained_networks_are_opaque
if: weights are produced by SGD on random init
then: their internal computation is not directly readable
rules.why: Mechanistic interpretability tries to recover structure post-hoc. The substrate's authored networks (Tracr-compiled) have the structure baked in by construction. Different paradigm: structure → weights vs weights → ? → behaviour.

rules.name: authored_networks_have_provable_properties
if: a network is compiled from declarative spec (Tracr)
then: its behaviour is provably exact for the specified input domain
rules.why: Compilation produces specific weights; spec defines behaviour; weights implement spec. The substrate's gadgets Mt instantiates this. Polar opposite of training's empirical fit. The substrate's preferred paradigm.

rules.name: ML_compute_dominates_economic_constraints
if: pretraining a frontier model costs $100M+
then: few organisations can do it
rules.why: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, a few others. Open source uses smaller scale + clever techniques. Compute concentration → power concentration. The bitter lesson asks compute; the substrate asks for structure.

rules.name: neurosymbolic_combines_paradigms
if: a system uses both neural pattern recognition + symbolic reasoning
then: it can be stronger than either alone
rules.why: AlphaGeometry: neural for proposing constructions + symbolic for verification. The substrate IS this: symbolic Mts + Tracr-compiled networks where useful. Acknowledging both paradigms have legitimate niches.

rules.name: training_is_one_paradigm_not_the_paradigm
if: a system needs to compute a function
then: training is one option; authoring is another
rules.why: Training: empirical, brute force, opaque, statistically fit, compute-bound. Authoring (Tracr): declarative, exact, queryable, structurally correct, design-bound. Different trade-offs; different problems suit each. The substrate prefers authoring.

rules.name: substrate_knows_ML_to_not_be_ML
if: substrate understands what training is + why it works
then: it can deliberately avoid the paradigm where authoring fits better
rules.why: Knowing the alternative makes the choice intentional. The substrate isn't an LLM; it's a graph-resident reasoning system. Understanding ML lets it interface with ML systems + know when authoring (its own paradigm) is the better answer.
